title: Test Your Understanding: Consistent Hashing
description: Trade-offs, remapping behavior, virtual nodes, and failure modes — not just definitions.

questions.question: You use `hash(key) % N` to route cache keys to N servers. You add one server (N → N+1). What happens to most existing keys?

options.text: They stay on the same server; only new keys use the new server
Roughly 1/(N+1) of keys move to the new server; the rest stay put
Nearly all keys remap to different servers because the modulus base changed
Keys are duplicated on both old and new servers until TTL expires

questions.explanation: Modulo hashing depends on N. When N changes, almost every key's remainder changes, so nearly all keys map to different servers — often causing a mass cache invalidation.

questions.question: In consistent hashing, how is a key assigned to a server?

options.text: The server with the lowest numeric ID
The first server encountered clockwise from the key's position on the hash ring
The server with the fewest keys currently stored
A random server chosen per request for load balance

questions.explanation: Keys and servers sit on a ring. A key belongs to the next server clockwise from its hash position. That localizes remapping when nodes join or leave.

questions.question: When you add one node to an N-node consistent hash ring, approximately what fraction of keys need to move?

options.text: Nearly 100%

questions.explanation: On average, the new node takes ownership of one (N+1)th of the keyspace — keys in the arcs it covers. The rest stay on their current servers.

questions.question: Why do production systems use virtual nodes (vnodes)?

options.text: To encrypt keys before hashing
To spread each physical server's ownership across many ring positions for more even load
To eliminate the need for key migration when nodes change
To guarantee strong consistency across shards

questions.explanation: A single point per server on the ring can create uneven arcs. Many vnodes per physical server smooth out ownership and improve load balance. Migration still happens when nodes change.

questions.question: A single cache key receives 40% of all traffic. Consistent hashing with perfect vnode balance is in place. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: Traffic automatically spreads across all nodes because hashing is even
The node owning that key still handles ~40% of traffic — hot keys are not fixed by consistent hashing alone
The key splits across shards automatically
Virtual nodes duplicate the key on every server

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing balances different keys across nodes. One extremely hot key still lands on one primary owner. Hot keys need app-level splitting, local caching, or replication — not just a better ring.

questions.question: A node fails and is removed from the ring. What happens to its keys?

options.text: They are lost unless a backup exists
They transfer to the next server clockwise on the ring
They redistribute uniformly to all remaining nodes instantly with no migration
They remain orphaned until the node rejoins

questions.explanation: When a node leaves, its vnodes disappear and keys in those arcs fall to the next clockwise server. That server must absorb the data and traffic — migration and capacity headroom still matter.

questions.question: Consistent hashing eliminates the need for background key migration when scaling a distributed cache.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing limits how many keys must move, not whether they move. Keys still need to be copied to new owners; large clusters can migrate terabytes over time.

questions.question: Which scenario is the strongest reason to adopt consistent hashing over modulo sharding?

options.text: You need range queries sorted by user ID across all shards
You expect to add or remove cache nodes without triggering a near-total invalidation
You have a single-server database with no plans to partition
You want the simplest possible routing logic for a fixed cluster size forever

questions.explanation: The main win is minimal remapping on resize — critical for caches and elastic shard counts. Range queries favor range sharding; fixed single-node setups don't need either.
